title: Lettre Tate (mai 66) (Cristaux) : lettre (1966), tapuscrit (s.d.), notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
This is Chapter 3, §3.1 of the May 1966 letter to Tate on crystals. Having concluded in Chapter 2 that crystals are 'too fine' for families of abelian varieties, Grothendieck turns to p-divisible (Barsotti–Tate) groups Φ over a base S on which p is locally nilpotent. He proposes to transpose his construction G(A) (the universal vector extension of an abelian scheme, after Serre and Rosenlicht) to this setting.

1. Hom(Φ, Ĝa) = 0. In particular Φ has no infinitesimal automorphisms.
2. The sheaf 'H^2 of Φ with values in Ĝa', in the sense of the group complex, is the same thing as Ext^1(Φ, Ĝa). It should be locally free of rank g* = dim Φ*, and canonically isomorphic to Lie(Φ*) = t_{Φ*}. He says this is suggested by the Lubin–Tate work on moduli of formal groups.
3. Hence there is a universal extension G(Φ) of Φ by a vector formal group. Its Lie algebra H(Φ) sits in an exact sequence (*): 0 → t^∨_{Φ*} → H(Φ) → t_Φ → 0. In modern notation this reads 0 → ω_{Φ*} → Lie E(Φ) → Lie Φ → 0. It is functorial in Φ and compatible with base change, and it plays the role of H^1_dR with its Hodge filtration.
4. G(Φ) 'varies less than Φ' under infinitesimal deformation. Even so, Grothendieck doubts that G(Φ) comes from a crystal of (more or less formal) groups, except perhaps at first order. He expects this only when Φ is an extension of an ind-étale group by a toric p-divisible group (the ordinary case), and he adds by hand 'and S reduced to a point (?)'.
5. He suggests studying deformations of Φ with the variation of G(Φ) held fixed by a crystal of groups.

On the next page this becomes the expectation that, over a complete DVR, lifts of Φ correspond to lifts of the Hodge filtration (*) inside the Dieudonné module. He also asks how to read off the Tate module of the generic fibre from such filtration data.
errors: Minor notational slip. The universal extension should be by the vector group of ω_{Φ*} = t^∨_{Φ*}, the dual of Ext^1(Φ, Ĝa) ≅ t_{Φ*}. He calls it 'the formal group (covariant) of t_{Φ*}', but the sequence (*) correctly has t^∨_{Φ*} as kernel.

The pessimism about crystallinity was later superseded. Messing (1972) and Mazur–Messing showed that Lie E(Φ), and in a suitable sense E(Φ), is crystalline on nilpotent divided-power thickenings for arbitrary p-divisible Φ and arbitrary base, not only in the ordinary case over a point. The obstruction he foresaw disappears once divided powers are imposed.
Ext^1(Φ, Ĝa) ≅ Lie(Φ*) is stated 'sauf erreur', without proof. It is true; Messing proves it.

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known 1966 letter to Tate, the genesis of the crystalline Dieudonné theory and the Grothendieck–Messing theorem. Its content is explicitly credited to Grothendieck by Messing and Mazur–Messing. The page's only distinctive feature is a transient pessimism about crystallinity before divided powers were introduced, which is of historical interest only.
transcription_corrections: The handwritten insertion replacing the struck 'p-divisibles' reads '± formels', i.e. 'cristal en groupes ± formels' (more or less formal groups).
The handwritten addition after 'torique,' reads 'et S réduit à un point (?).'
The typed word is 'sût' corrected to 'sûr'; the bracket notation in the transcription inverts this.
In 'le faisceau en modules', 'groupes' is struck and 'modules' written above.
